title: TubeSaku WebMCP
pitch: TubeSaku turns Japanese YouTube data into WebMCP tools: agents discover live streams or cover-song opportunities, then render their personalized picks back into the site.
about_excerpt: TubeSaku turns Japanese YouTube data into WebMCP tools: agents discover live streams or cover-song opportunities, then render their personalized picks back into the site. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector ChatGPT - Codex Inspiration YouTube’s recommendation algorithms are highly sophisticated, yet there are still situations where users struggle to find exactly what they want—for example, finding the right upcoming live stream at a specific time, or identifying a song that is popular but not already overcrowded with cover videos. We operate TubeSaku , a website that collects and organizes Japanese YouTube data for creators and viewers. As the amount of data grew, however, we encountered a new problem: more data did not always make decisions easier. Users could see rankings, schedules, demand signals, and historical observations, but still had to decide where to start. That led to the first idea behind TubeSaku WebMCP: Let the website remain the expert on its domain data, while an external AI agent becomes the expert on the individual user. The agent can understand what the user actually wants, query TubeSaku's structured evidence, compare the candidates, and then return its selections—and the reasons for those selections—back into the TubeSaku interface. There was also a broader motivation. AI is changing how people discover information on the web. Independent research from Pew Research Center found that users who encountered an AI-generated search summary clicked traditional search results less often than users who did not, while Google has reported that overall organic click volume remains relatively stable and that the clicks it sends are increasingly high-quality. The exact aggregate impact is still debated, but the underlying incentive question is important for the open web: What happens if websites continue producing useful information, but users increasingly consume the answer somewhere else without visiting the source? For many websites, a visit is not only a click. It is how users discover a new service, understand who created the information, build trust, see related features, subscribe, purchase, or take another action. TubeSaku WebMCP explores a different relationship between websites and AI agents: instead of treating the website only as raw material for an answer generated elsewhere, the agent can enter the first-party experience, use capabilities explicitly provided by the site, and make that site more useful for the user. What it does TubeSaku currently offers two WebMCP workflows. Live Schedule The first is designed for viewers. Agents can search TubeSaku's Japanese YouTube live-stream data using criteria such as: date time keyword category debut status For example, a user can ask: “Find three gaming live streams tomorrow evening that look interesting.” The agent searches TubeSaku, compares the returned candidates against the user's request, and then calls a second WebMCP tool to display its choices directly on the TubeSaku page as AI Picks . The agent can also provide a short explanation for each selection. Those reasons are rendered inside TubeSaku alongside the underlying stream information. So the result is not only: agent → answer in chat but: agent → decision → explanation → personalized first-party page Cover-song Planner The second workflow is designed for VTubers, YouTubers, vsingers, and singers deciding what song to cover next. TubeSaku combines several kinds of evidence, including: Japanese YouTube Charts recent cover-song upload activity historical cover availability where observed existing cover performance early-stage spread signals such as Shorts growth The agent can answer questions such as: “Find popular Japanese songs that are not currently overcrowded with new covers.” TubeSaku does not hard-code one universal recommendation. Instead, it exposes the evidence. The agent decides how those signals should be weighted for this particular user. A creator seeking maximum demand might choose differently from a small VTuber looking for a less competitive opportunity. At the time of submission, the live Cover Planner dataset compared 154 tracked songs against 4,891 recent cover observations from 3,439 YouTube channels. After making its decision, the agent can create AI Cover Picks directly inside TubeSaku, explain why each song was selected, and build an in-page listening playlist from validated existing YouTube cover videos. This also enables cross-lingual use. An English-speaking user can ask a question in English, the agent can reason over TubeSaku's Japanese data, explain its recommendation in English, and still preserve the original Japanese song and video titles. How we built it Hackathon scope TubeSaku.com and its YouTube data pipeline existed before this challenge. During the WebMCP Challenge submission period, we added the WebMCP layer shown in this submission: search_live_streams show_live_streams search_cover_songs show_cover_playlist first-party AI Picks interfaces agent-generated selection explanations an in-page cover-song listening playlist a standalone runnable demo using sample data The public repository and dated commit history document the work completed during the challenge period. A production data pipeline was already in place for TubeSaku. Local collectors and GCP-based jobs gather and clean observational data about YouTube in Japan, including live-stream schedules, YouTube Charts, recently uploaded cover videos, and observations of existing cover-song supply. The WebMCP Challenge WebMCP gave us a lightweight way to expose selected capabilities from that system directly to browser agents. Both workflows use the same pattern: TubeSaku first-party data ↓ WebMCP search tool ↓ Agent combines evidence with user context ↓ WebMCP show tool ↓ TubeSaku first-party UI Live Schedule Live demo search_live_streams → agent compares candidates → show_live_streams → AI Picks + selection reasons Cover-song Planner Live demo search_cover_songs → agent compares demand and supply evidence → show_cover_playlist → AI Cover Picks + reasons + Listening Playlist We deliberately separate the search and display tools. The display tools only accept IDs that appeared in the most recent search result. An agent therefore cannot arbitrarily inject unrelated streams or songs into the page. Selection explanations are also associated with those validated IDs and rendered as text rather than trusted HTML. For the Cover Planner, URLs exposed to the UI are validated, and listening examples are filtered before being exposed to the agent/player using checks including duration, obvious dance/clip false positives, public availability, and embeddability. We also made the tool execution wrappers tolerant of browser implementations that invoke a WebMCP tool without an optional execution-context argument, which improved interoperability during testing across agent browsers. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was data quality. Searching YouTube for Japanese cover-song terminology can also return: dance Shorts clips tutorials instrumental videos commentary unrelated songs with similar titles videos that technically match the query but are useless as listening examples We therefore added multiple validation layers instead of trusting YouTube search results directly. We also learned that browser lifecycle and first-party page architecture matter. TubeSaku serves some pages as generated static HTML, so modifying a template did not necessarily update the deployed page immediately. Playlist development exposed another set of subtle issues. YouTube's embed playlist behavior did not match our initial assumptions, and dynamically initializing the IFrame Player API behaved differently inside an agent browser than in our minimal local environment. We eventually simplified the implementation. TubeSaku keeps the validated selected video IDs itself and changes a standard YouTube iframe when the user presses Previous or Next. That solution was both simpler and more reliable. Browser interoperability also produced a useful lesson: different WebMCP-capable environments do not necessarily supply every optional execution argument in exactly the same way. We adjusted our tools defensively and added regression tests for this case. Accomplishments that we're proud of We achieved a complete end-to-end WebMCP interaction on the live TubeSaku website: natural-language request → WebMCP search → agent reasoning → validated selection → WebMCP UI action → first-party TubeSaku update The latest version goes one step further. The agent does not only return its selections—it can return the reason for each selection , and those explanations become part of the TubeSaku page. The Cover Planner is especially exciting because the user can immediately inspect and listen to the evidence behind a recommendation while continuing the conversation with the agent.
